title: Who enters this tournament?
hook: Would a gender difference in competition travel unchanged across societies?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Inspect reversal across social settings rather than interpreting one sample as biological destiny.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Inspect reversal across social settings rather than interpreting one sample as biological destiny.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: In an illustrative context, 60% of women and 40% of men enter a competition. What is the women-minus-men gap? Toy inputs A=[60, 40]; B=[30, 50].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[20, 60, 40], [-20, 30, 50]]. Labels: Women−men pp, Women %, Men %.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The sign of the gap changes across the two supplied contexts. A single sample’s ordering is therefore not a context-free law in this comparison. The toy table does not establish why any real society has a particular pattern.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Women entering %=30, Men entering %=50. What is Women−men pp? Answer: -20.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Women entering %=30, Men entering %=50. What is Women−men pp?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives -20. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: Women in matrilineal Khasi society chose to compete more often than men, the reverse of the patriarchal Maasai (Gneezy, Leonard & List, 2009).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Inspect reversal across social settings rather than interpreting one sample as biological destiny.
